note.question: How should a large cloud provider jointly price computing speed and interruption risk, and when do scale, user mobility, and platform competition sustain or eliminate strategic throttling of lower-tier users?
note.overview: A cloud provider designs a price-quality menu to screen users whose willingness to pay and delay sensitivity are private, subject to incentive compatibility and capacity. The paper derives the optimal throttling mechanism, gives a weakly dominant-strategy pay-as-bid implementation, and characterizes price-quality equilibrium under platform competition.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: In the monopoly mechanism, the provider commits to a menu that maps reported user types into computing speed, interruption probability, and pay-per-use price. Users privately observe their types and select or report a contract; jobs then arrive and are processed in the large shared queue subject to the induced interruption and capacity rules. In the pay-as-bid implementation, the provider commits to a spot-price distribution and users bid before each price realization. In the duopoly extension, two platforms simultaneously compete in price-quality menus and users choose between them or their outside option.

components.label: Provider-optimal incentive-compatible mechanism with weakly dominant pay-as-bid implementation
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Provider-optimal incentive-compatible mechanism with weakly dominant pay-as-bid implementation. Problem (P) optimizes over incentive-compatible and individually rational direct mechanisms. Theorem 2 characterizes the optimal allocation, and Proposition 2 shows that, when the provider commits to the specified price distribution, bidding b=p*(θ) is weakly dominant, implements r*(θ), and forms a Bayes-Nash implementation. Theorem 3 separately characterizes symmetric price-quality equilibria under duopoly.
